The bill would create a new Commonwealth Act to clarify how Queensland's G20 safety law interacts with federal law at Brisbane Airport during the 2014 G20 Summit.
It would provide mechanisms for resolving overlaps between the Queensland G20 Act and existing Commonwealth legislation at the airport, which is a Commonwealth place.
The bill would ensure police and authorised persons clearly understand which powers they can use at Brisbane Airport during the summit.

Police officers and other appointed or authorised persons at Brisbane Airport during the G20 Summit.

Jacinta Collins Labor will be supporting the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill 2014. On 15 and 16 November this year Brisbane will play host to arguably the most significant world leaders' summit, the G20. G20 members account for two-thirds of the world's population, around 80 per cent of global trade and, most notably, 85 per cent of the world's economy. Geographically, all the world's populated regions will be represented. The event itself is expected to have around 3,000 media representatives and around 4,000 delegates attend. It will place Brisbane at the centre of the world's attention at that time. It is a significant event that has as been brought to Australia by the previous government, which I will speak about in a moment. The G20 is the place to discuss global economic and financial matters. The objects of the G20 are threefold: to modernise international financial architecture, to promote financial regulations that reduce risks and prevent future financial crises, and policy coordination between its members in order to achieve global economic stability and sustainable growth. The bill itself clarifies the interaction between the Queensland government's G20 (Safety and Security) Act 2013 and the stand-alone bill proposed here. It was determined by the Queensland government that a separate act was needed because of the extra duties the Queensland Police Service would be facing. Those duties include: security for accommodation venues where meetings are being held, security for official parties and world leaders, motorcade routes and for other official events. That is on top of the everyday work the Queensland Police Service do in providing policing for the general public. The extra powers granted under the Queensland act and this bill are similar to the ones granted to the APEC meeting in New South Wales in 2007 and the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in 2011. Moved a bill to clarify police and security powers at Brisbane Airport during the G20 leaders summit in November, noting G20 member countries represent around 85 per cent of global GDP. Said the legislation would sunset the day after the summit ends to avoid the need for later repeal.

Endorsed the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill to counter extremist protesters at the Brisbane summit, and argued the G20, representing about 85 per cent of global GDP and 75 per cent of global trade, benefits developing nations that anti-globalisation protesters wrongly claim to defend.

Confirmed Labor's support for the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill, said the November summit is expected to draw as many as 4,000 delegates and 3,000 media representatives, and credited former Prime Minister Julia Gillard with securing Australia's hosting rights at the 2011 Cannes G20 summit.

Detailed the committee's sixth report covering 18 bills and 175 legislative instruments, and flagged concerns that the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill 2014 would roll back Commonwealth law at Brisbane Airport during the November G20 summit without a human rights assessment of the Queensland provisions being applied.

Supported the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill 2014, welcomed Brisbane's hosting of the November G20 leaders meeting expecting about 7,000 foreign leaders, staff and media, and urged the summit prioritise inclusive infrastructure and action on tax avoidance.

Supported the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill 2014 and promoted Brisbane's hosting of the November 2014 G20 Leaders Summit, citing an expected 4,000 delegates and 3,000 media and forecasting economic benefits worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

Supported the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill 2014 and defended Australian intelligence agencies' surveillance powers against criticism following Edward Snowden's leaks, citing US Judge William Pauley's ruling that bulk metadata collection had helped disrupt terrorist attacks.

Summed up debate on the G20 (Safety and Security) Complementary Bill, thanked Labor for its support while criticising the Greens for opposing it in the Senate, and said the bill aligns Commonwealth and Queensland law enforcement powers at Brisbane Airport ahead of the G20 Leaders Summit in November.
